evidence_quotes.quote: A purposeful sample of 34 (n = 34) participants was selected, based on participants’ knowledge and experience as end-users and stakeholders in the district municipality’s water governance.
In determining access equity, the study established that a significant number of residents in the district municipality still lack access to safe drinking water and proper sanitation.

Findings indicate that intermittent water supply in Amathole District Municipality is unreliable and unpredictable. Inconsistencies in the water provision interventions adversely affect municipal residents on the margins.

We have embarked on several interventions including drilling boreholes, constructing dams, and refurbishing water treatment plants and water carting to communities that do not have the infrastructure.
The researchers examined stakeholder participation and adherence to governance principles of openness and accountability, as these are key tools used to ensure procedural fairness.

Nonetheless, the study also revealed gaps in procedural fairness, emanating from limited transparency, accountability, and limited voice and involvement of stakeholders, mainly in disadvantaged and marginalised rural communities.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to drinking water services (and reports municipal sanitation coverage statistics) across rural and urban communities in Amathole District Municipality.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this paper would qualify (plain=yes) because it examines municipal water governance and procedural fairness, including stakeholder participation in Integrated Development Plan (IDP) processes, ward councillor accountability, financial audit performance, and intergovernmental coordination between district and local municipalities. Under the mandatory narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, it fails (narrow=no): the empirical analysis does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, indigent registration, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, frontline discretion/accommodation, disconnection/enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory rules governing access). Instead, it evaluates generic municipal infrastructure project delivery (boreholes, dams, standpipes, water carting, access roads for maintenance) and broad participatory governance/accountability background.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains original qualitative empirical data from two focus group discussions with community members (n = 14), semi-structured interviews with municipal and water sector officials (n = 20), participant observation, and secondary municipal IDP/audit records.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative and descriptive secondary outcomes on household/community water access disparities, reliance on rivers and rainwater harvesting, intermittent water supply, inconsistent water tanker deliveries, and non-functioning rural boreholes and schemes.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and sample (communities and water governance officials in Amathole District Municipality, Eastern Cape, n = 34, plus municipal-level secondary data), the broad governance/project-delivery exposure studied, water access/reliability outcomes, and an exploratory qualitative case study design.

study_design: Exploratory qualitative case study (focus group discussions, semi-structured interviews, participant observation, and document review)
population_and_sample: Amathole District Municipality (Eastern Cape Province, South Africa); purposeful sample of n = 34 participants (14 community members in two focus group discussions and 20 municipal/Water Board officials and councillors in semi-structured interviews), supplemented by municipal IDP records.
exposure: Broad municipal water governance and social equity dimensions (IDP public participation roadshows, municipal transparency/audit accountability, intergovernmental project coordination, and rural infrastructure/water-carting interventions), with no specific rule-type legal or administrative access mechanism examined.
outcome: Rural-urban disparities in household/community water service access, intermittent water supply, inconsistent water tanker filling, and reliance on untreated surface water or rainwater harvesting.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this qualitative case study empirically examines rural-urban disparities in municipal water service access and reliability in South Africa (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type scope clarification. Rather than analyzing a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing household or community access (e.g., tariff or Free Basic Water eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burdens, enforcement, or regulatory structure governing access), the study assesses generic municipal infrastructure delivery (borehole drilling, water carting, O&M, road access for construction) and broad public administration governance principles (IDP consultation formalities, councillor responsiveness, and municipal audit accountability).
